## Introduction to Spatial Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
We are going to build geographic maps in R. To do this, we work with spatial vectors.

Standard dataframes hold text and numbers. Spatial dataframes hold geometries:

\- **Points:** A specific animal sighting or a single tree.

\- **Lines:** Rivers, roads, or animal movement tracks.

\- **Polygons:** State boundaries, lakes, or oceans.

(Why do paper maps never win at poker? Because they always fold).
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
FIGURE
:::
:::::

## The Spatial Toolkit

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
To handle these geometries, we need libraries that bridge the gap between geographic data and the `tidyverse`.

- `sf` (Simple Features): backbone of R spatial analysis. It makes maps act like dataframes.
- `tigris`: Pulls accurate US boundaries (states, counties) directly from the Census Bureau.
- `rnaturalearth`: Provides global boundaries, including Canada, lakes, and oceans.
- `rinat`: Pulls community-science observations directly from iNaturalist.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
# Install if needed:
# install.packages(c("sf", "tigris", "rnaturalearth", "rinat"))

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rinat)
```
:::
:::::

## Map Projections: Flattening the Earth

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
The Earth is a 3D sphere. Our screens are flat. A map projection is the mathematical formula used to flatten the Earth.

Every projection distorts something: area, shape, distance, or direction. In R, changing a projection means recalculating the underlying grid. We define projections using a Coordinate Reference System (CRS), often assigned via an EPSG code or a PROJ4 string. We ensure all our map layers share the exact same CRS so they align perfectly.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
figure
:::
:::::

## Fetching the Base Map

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
First, we pull the political and physical boundaries. We filter the data to the specific states and provinces we want.

Notice how we use st_transform() to set a uniform projection. Here, we use EPSG 4269 (NAD83), which is standard for North American mapping.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
### US States

midwest <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") %>% 
  filter(STUSPS %in% c("MN", "WI", "MI", "ND", "SD", "IA")) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)

### Canadian Provinces

canada <- ne_states(country = "Canada", returnclass = "sf") %>% 
  filter(name %in% c("Ontario", "Manitoba")) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)

### Major Lakes

lakes <- ne_download(scale = 50, type = "lakes", 
                     category = "physical", 
                     returnclass = "sf") %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)
```
:::
:::::

## Fetching Fisher Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Fishers (Pekania pennanti) are a key mustelid in Minnesota's forests. We will query recent observations from iNaturalist using rinat.

The data comes in as a standard dataframe (latitude/longitude columns). We use st_as_sf() to convert those columns into a recognized spatial point geometry.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
# Get iNaturalist data Pekania pennanti 
fisher_raw <- get_inat_obs(taxon_name = "Hemimysis anomala", 
                           bounds = c(40, -100, 50, -85), 
                           maxresults = 200)

# Convert to a spatial object
fisher_sf <- st_as_sf(fisher_raw, 
                      coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
                      crs = 4326) %>% # 4326 is standard GPS coordinates
  st_transform(crs = 4269) # Match the base map projection

```
:::
:::::

## Building the Map (Points)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Mapping in sf relies on geom_sf(). We stack layers exactly like a lasagna. Bottom layers first (land), top layers last (points).

We use coord_sf() to zoom the "camera lens" to our specific bounding box.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = midwest, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "aliceblue", color = "lightblue") +
  geom_sf(data = fisher_sf, color = "darkred", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-100, -85), ylim = c(40, 50), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fisher Sightings in the Midwest",
       caption = "Data: iNaturalist")

```
:::
:::::

## Distribution Heatmaps

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Points are great, but dense clusters become illegible. We can use a 2D kernel density estimate (a heatmap) to highlight distribution hotspots.

To use stat_density_2d(), we extract the raw coordinates back out of our spatial object, then map the calculated density (after_stat(level)) to a color gradient.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
# Extract raw coordinates for the density function
fisher_coords <- fisher_sf %>%
  mutate(lon = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
         lat = st_coordinates(.)[,2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "grey20", color = "grey50") +
  geom_sf(data = midwest, fill = "grey20", color = "grey50") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "black", color = NA) +
  stat_density_2d(data = fisher_coords, 
                  aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = after_stat(level)), 
                  geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-100, -85), ylim = c(40, 50), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fisher Sighting Density",
       fill = "Density")
```
:::
:::::

## Fetching Fisher Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
Fishers (Pekania pennanti) are a key mustelid in Minnesota's forests. We will query recent observations from iNaturalist using the rinat API.

The data comes in as a standard dataframe of latitude and longitude columns. We use st_as_sf() to convert those columns into a recognized spatial point geometry.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
# Get iNaturalist data
fisher_raw <- get_inat_obs(taxon_name = "Pekania pennanti", 
                           bounds = c(40, -100, 50, -85), 
                           maxresults = 500)

# Convert to a spatial object
fisher_sf <- st_as_sf(fisher_raw, 
                      coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
                      crs = 4326) %>% # 4326 is standard GPS coordinates
  st_transform(crs = 4269) # Match the base map projection
```
:::
:::::

## Building the Map (Points)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Mapping in sf relies on geom_sf(). We stack layers exactly like a lasagna. Bottom layers first (land), top layers last (the animals).

We use coord_sf() to zoom the "camera lens" to our specific bounding box so the map isn't awkwardly zoomed out.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| fig.height: 5
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = midwest, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "aliceblue", color = "lightblue") +
  geom_sf(data = fisher_sf, color = "darkred", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-100, -85), ylim = c(40, 50), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fisher Sightings in the Midwest",
       caption = "Data: iNaturalist")


```
:::
:::::
